Consult Summary:
- Adult female with sudden-onset left-sided headache beginning this morning with blurred vision/“zigzag” visual phenomena, dizziness, photophobia, nausea and two episodes of vomiting — clinician provisionally diagnosed migraine with aura and advised analgesia/antiemetic and follow-up assessment.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Sudden-onset, severe left-sided headache (around/behind the left eye) that began this morning (~4 hours prior to consultation).
  - Associated blurred vision and transient visual phenomena described as “zigzag lines” (patient’s description consistent with visual aura).
  - Dizziness, photophobia/intolerance of screens.
  - Nausea with two episodes of vomiting (one at headache onset and another shortly after); ongoing nausea.
  - Headache worse with movement; patient prefers to keep head still.
- Timeline / progression:
  - Onset: sudden this morning, approximately 4 hours before the consult.
  - Course: persistent since onset; paracetamol taken ~1 hour after onset (~3 hours prior to consult) without improvement; patient reports slight subjective improvement but still symptomatic.
- Exacerbating / relieving factors:
  - Worsened by movement; screens exacerbate symptoms (photophobia).
  - Paracetamol did not provide relief.
  - GP recommended trial of ibuprofen plus an antiemetic and oral fluids/sugary carbonated drink (per clinician advice).
- Associated symptoms / review of systems mentioned:
  - Visual aura (zigzag lines), blurred vision.
  - Dizziness, nausea, vomiting.
  - No weakness of arms/legs reported.
  - Able to walk in a straight line; no gait disturbance reported.
  - No fever, neck stiffness, speech disturbance, sensory loss, or loss of consciousness mentioned.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No prior headaches like this previously (first such episode per patient).
  - No regular medications.
  - No known drug allergies.
  - Pregnancy felt unlikely by patient.
  - No reported focal neurological deficits.

Past Medical History:
- Personal:
  - History of kidney stones (patient reported past kidney stone).
  - No other chronic medical conditions reported.
- Family:
  - Mother with migraine.
  - Mother with hypothyroidism.

Medications:
- Taken during episode:
  - Paracetamol — dose/route/frequency not documented (patient reports it was ineffective).
- Recommended by clinician:
  - Ibuprofen — dose/route/frequency not documented (recommended).
  - Antiemetic / “anti-sickness” — specific agent and dose/route/frequency not documented (recommended).
  - Oral sugary/carbonated drink (e.g., Coke) recommended as adjunct.
- Regular medications: none reported.
- Allergies:
  - No known drug allergies (patient reports “not that I'm aware”).

Social History:
- Patient identification:
  - Name: Maria; DOB given as “22 March (ninety)” (as stated by patient).
- Occupation / living situation: not documented.
- Tobacco / alcohol / recreational drug use: not documented.
- Financial or lifestyle factors: not documented.

Family History:
- Mother: migraine and hypothyroidism.
- No other relevant family history elicited.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings:
  - No formal recorded neurological exam results beyond history.
  - Clinician noted no reported limb weakness and that patient is walking normally (no gait disturbance) based on history.
  - No other exam findings documented.

Investigations:
- None performed or ordered during this consultation.
- No imaging, labs, or formal neurological testing documented.
- Clinician advised further assessment (neurological exam) if symptoms persist or worsen.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Probable migraine with visual aura (clinician’s provisional diagnosis, supported by DDx ranking).
- DDx Integration (top 2–3 from provided DDx, consistent with transcript):
  1. Migraine with aura — High likelihood.
     - Supporting: Unilateral left-sided headache; visual “zigzag” phenomena (aura); photophobia (screen intolerance); nausea and vomiting; worsened by movement; family history of migraine; no focal deficits reported.
     - Opposing: First episode of this type (de novo presentation possible).
  2. Basilar-type / vestibular migraine — Medium likelihood.
     - Supporting: Prominent dizziness, visual disturbance, vomiting without focal deficits.
     - Opposing: No brainstem signs (dysarthria, ataxia, bilateral findings) reported; less commonly a first-time presentation.
  3. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) — Low to medium likelihood (must be considered for sudden severe headaches).
     - Supporting: Sudden onset and vomiting.
     - Opposing: Headache not described as “worst-ever” (patient rates ~6/10), no loss of consciousness, no neck stiffness or focal neurological signs reported.
  - No conflict noted between transcript and DDx.

Issue 1: Acute severe unilateral headache with visual aura — probable migraine with aura
- Assessment:
  - Clinical features most consistent with migraine with visual aura given unilateral headache, scintillating/zigzag visual phenomena, photophobia, nausea/vomiting, and family history.
- Plan:
  - Symptomatic treatment trial at home:
    - Analgesia: trial of ibuprofen (recommended by clinician) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Antiemetic (recommended) — agent and dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Oral hydration and consideration of sugary carbonated drink (e.g., Coke) as advised by clinician.
  - If symptoms improve, patient may cancel the planned assessment appointment.
  - If symptoms persist despite treatment, or if there is no improvement by the time of scheduled assessment, return for full in-person neurological examination.
  - Safety-net / red flag advice (verbalized by clinician; document and reinforce):
    - Return immediately / attend ED if any of the following occur: sudden worsening to “worst-ever” headache, new focal neurological deficits (weakness, numbness, speech disturbance), loss of consciousness, progressive drowsiness, neck stiffness, high fever, or ongoing uncontrolled vomiting/ dehydration.
  - Consider urgent neuroimaging (noncontrast head CT) and further investigations (e.g., lumbar puncture) if red flags arise or if exam is abnormal — recommended as indicated (per DDx consideration for SAH/other intracranial pathology).

Issue 2: Nausea and vomiting
- Assessment:
  - Secondary to migraine-associated autonomic symptoms.
- Plan:
  - Antiemetic recommended (specific medication not documented); clinician advised obtaining anti-sickness from pharmacy or via prescription.
  - Encourage small sips of fluids; antiemetic to facilitate oral analgesia.

Issue 3: Patient anxiety / concern about serious intracranial pathology (tumour, stroke)
- Assessment:
  - Patient expressed significant anxiety and concern about brain tumour or stroke.
- Plan:
  - Reassurance that presentation is most consistent with migraine but that serious causes must be excluded if red flags or neurological deficits develop.
  - Offer and arrange prompt in-person neurological assessment today if symptoms persist or worsen; patient advised to attend A&E urgently if red flags develop.
  - Patient instructed to contact clinic to cancel appointment if symptoms resolve after treatment.

General plan items:
- Follow-up:
  - Planned clinic assessment / neurological exam arranged (time not documented); patient may cancel if symptoms resolve.
- Documentation of patient education: discussed typical migraine features, expected time course (may resolve within minutes to hours, but migraines can last 4–72 hours), and stepped treatment options.
- No investigations were performed during this consult; consider imaging only if red flags, abnormal neurological exam, or failure to improve.

Quality checks:
- Missing but expected elements:
  - Vitals were not recorded.
  - No formal documented neurological examination (only history of no weakness and normal walking).
  - Medication doses, routes and frequencies for paracetamol (already taken), ibuprofen and antiemetic were not documented.
  - No contact details/times for planned follow-up appointment documented in transcript.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None identified — DDx (migraine with aura highest likelihood) is consistent with clinician impression and transcript.
- Transcript quality:
  - Mostly clear clinical history; brief loss of connection noted during consultation.
